question.problem: William has a desk with three drawers, $A,$ $B,$ and $C.$ In drawer $A,$ he has $14$ markers, of which $3$ are red. In drawer $B,$ he has $18$ markers, of which $4$ are red. And, in drawer $C,$ he has $20$ markers, of which $6$ are red. If one marker is selected at random from all the markers combined, what is the probability that it is red?
question.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be the event that a chosen marker is red, and 

- let $A$ be the event that the marker was from drawer $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the marker was from drawer $B,$

- let $C$ be the event that the marker was from drawer $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A⊔B⊔C$ covers the entire sample space.

To calculate the probability that a randomly selected marker is red, we use the law of total probability:

$$
P(R)=P(R\cap A)+P(R\cap B)+P(R\cap C)
$$

First, notice that William has a total of 

$$
14+18+20=52
$$

markers in all three drawers.

- To calculate $P(R\cap A),$ we take the number of markers in the first drawer that are red $(3)$ and divide by the total number of markers $(52).$ So, we have

$$
P(R\cap A)=\frac{3}{52}.
$$

- To calculate $P(R\cap B),$ we take the number of markers in the second drawer that are red $(4)$ and divide by the total number of markers $(52).$ So, we have

$$
P(R\cap B)=\frac{4}{52}.
$$

- To calculate $P(R\cap C),$ we take the number of markers in the third drawer that are red $(6)$ and divide by the total number of markers $(52).$ So, we have

$$
P(R\cap C)=\frac{6}{52}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above information into the law of total probability, the probability that a randomly selected marker is red is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R\cap A)+P(R\cap B)+P(R\cap C) \\  & =\frac{3}{52}+\frac{4}{52}+\frac{6}{52} \\  & =\frac{13}{52} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
